points.title: Place value and number base
points.must: Place-value system: each position has a weight; rightmost = 1, each place to the left × base; value = sum of digit × place value. Base = number of digits and the multiplier between places.
points.model: Place value — the weight of a position; rightmost place value is 1, each place to the left = previous × base. Number base — the number of different digits a system uses (base b uses digits 0 … b−1). Example: 307 = 3×100 + 0×10 + 7×1.

points.title: Binary, denary and hexadecimal: definitions
points.must: Each system with its base, digits and place values (binary 2: 0–1, 1,2,4…128; denary 10: 0–9, 1,10,100; hex 16: 0–9 A–F, 1,16,256) and A=10 … F=15.
points.model: Binary — base 2, digits 0 and 1, place values 1, 2, 4, 8, 16, 32, 64, 128. Denary — base 10, digits 0–9, place values 1, 10, 100, 1000. Hexadecimal — base 16, digits 0–9 and A–F (A=10, B=11, C=12, D=13, E=14, F=15), place values 1, 16, 256, 4096.

points.title: Same digits, different bases
points.must: The example 1011 read in denary, binary and hex (1011, 11, 4113) and why the base must be shown (subscript, 0x, #).
points.model: 1011 in denary = 1011; in binary = 8+2+1 = 11; in hex = 4096+16+1 = 4113. Always show the base: 1011₂, 0x1011, B6₁₆, #B6.

points.title: Explaining the differences
points.must: Five points of difference: base/digits, place values, length of a number (182 = 10110110 = 182 = B6), who uses each, link to binary (16 = 2⁴, 10 is not a power of 2).
points.model: 1) Base and digits differ (2 / 10 / 16). 2) Place values grow ×2, ×10, ×16. 3) Smaller base → longer number: 182 = 10110110₂ (8 digits) = 182 (3) = B6 (2). 4) Binary used by hardware, denary by people, hex by programmers as short form of binary. 5) 16 = 2⁴ so 1 hex digit = 4 bits; 10 is not a power of 2 so denary ↔ binary needs arithmetic.

points.title: Why computers use binary
points.must: Transistors have two states (on/off, high/low voltage) = 1 and 0; two states are reliable despite noise, cheap and fast; storage media have two states; logic gates work with two values.
points.model: Computers use binary because transistors are switches with two states (on/off, high/low voltage) representing 1 and 0. Two states are easy to tell apart even with electrical noise → reliable, cheap, fast. Storage also has two states: magnetised two directions (HDD), pits/lands (CD), charge/no charge (flash). Logic gates work with true/false.

points.title: All data is binary
points.must: Numbers, text, images, sound and instructions are all stored as bit patterns; the program decides what a pattern means (01000001 = 65 or 'A').
points.model: Numbers, characters, pixels, sound samples and program instructions are all stored as bit patterns. The same pattern can mean different things: 01000001 = 65 or the letter 'A'.

points.title: Bit, nibble, byte
points.must: Definitions: bit = one binary digit; nibble = 4 bits (one hex digit, 0–15); byte = 8 bits (0–255).
points.model: Bit — a binary digit, 0 or 1, the smallest unit of data. Nibble — 4 bits = one hex digit (0–15). Byte — 8 bits, 256 values (0–255).

points.title: Number of values in n bits
points.must: n bits give 2ⁿ values and the largest value is 2ⁿ − 1; why one more bit doubles the number of patterns; table of powers of 2.
points.model: n bits store 2ⁿ different values; largest unsigned value = 2ⁿ − 1 (one pattern is 0). Each extra bit doubles the patterns (put 0 or 1 in front of every old pattern). 4 bits → 16 values, max 15; 8 bits → 256, max 255; 16 bits → 65 536, max 65 535.

points.title: Binary → denary
points.must: Method: write place values 128 … 1 above the bits (line up on the right), add the place values of the 1-bits; example with working.
points.model: Write 128 64 32 16 8 4 2 1 above the bits (rightmost bit = 1). Add the place values where the bit is 1. Example: 01011010 = 64 + 16 + 8 + 2 = 90.

points.title: Denary → binary: subtraction method
points.must: Largest place value first: if it fits write 1 and subtract, else 0; repeat to 1; example (156 = 10011100) and check by converting back.
points.model: Start at 128: if it fits write 1 and subtract, else write 0; repeat for 64, 32 … 1. Example 156: 128 (r 28), 64 no, 32 no, 16 (r 12), 8 (r 4), 4 (r 0), 2 no, 1 no → 10011100. Check: 128+16+8+4 = 156.

points.title: Denary → binary: division method
points.must: Divide by 2 repeatedly, write remainders, read them bottom up; why the first remainder is the rightmost bit; comparison with the subtraction method.
points.model: Divide by 2, write the remainder (0/1), divide the quotient again until 0; read remainders from the bottom up. The first remainder shows odd/even = the rightmost bit. Subtraction method works from the largest place value (good up to 255); division method from the smallest bit (good for large numbers).

points.title: Counting in binary, MSB and LSB, leading zeros
points.must: Counting 0–15 in 4 bits; 100…0 = power of 2, 11…1 = power of 2 minus 1; MSB = leftmost (largest place value), LSB = rightmost (place value 1); leading zeros keep a fixed size (5 = 00000101).
points.model: Count: 0000, 0001, 0010, 0011 … 1111 (15). 1000 = 8, 1111 = 15, 11111111 = 255. MSB — leftmost bit, largest place value (128 in a byte). LSB — rightmost bit, place value 1, odd/even. Leading zeros do not change the value but keep the fixed number of bits: 5 in a byte = 00000101.

points.title: Minimum number of bits
points.must: Rule: smallest n with 2ⁿ − 1 ≥ largest value (or 2ⁿ ≥ number of values); examples (150 lockers → 8 bits; 500 → 9 bits; 64 → 7 bits).
points.model: Find the first power of 2 greater than the largest value; its exponent is the number of bits. 150 lockers (0–149): 2⁷ = 128 too few, 2⁸ = 256 → 8 bits. Largest value 500 → 512 = 2⁹ → 9 bits. Value 64 → 6 bits reach only 63 → 7 bits.

points.title: Worked example: IPv4 address
points.must: An IPv4 address is 4 bytes (each 0–255); conversion of each part to 8-bit binary with leading zeros.
points.model: 192.168.10.37 = 11000000.10101000.00001010.00100101 (32 bits, 4 bytes). Each part must be 0–255; 300 is impossible because it does not fit in a byte.

points.title: Common mistakes
points.must: Remainders read bottom up; rightmost bit is worth 1; give all 8 bits; 8 bits store 256 values but max 255; MSB is on the left.
points.model: Read division remainders bottom up. Rightmost bit = 1. '8-bit answer' → write all 8 bits with leading 0s. 8 bits: 256 values, largest 255. MSB is the leftmost bit.
